idea-plugin.name: spek - OpenSpec Viewer
idea-plugin.description:
spek is an OpenSpec content viewer that lets you browse specs, changes, and task progress directly within your IDE.

Features:

  • Specs Browser — Browse spec documents with BDD syntax highlighting (WHEN/GIVEN, THEN, AND, MUST/SHALL)
  • Changes Browser — View changes with a tab per artifact the change contains (custom OpenSpec schemas supported), with the change's schema shown as a badge; rows surface creation/archive dates and lifecycle duration
  • Timeline — Horizontal Gantt-style chart of every change's lifecycle, with optional spec-topic grouping and an auto-scaling time axis
  • Task Progress — Track task completion with section-grouped progress bars
  • Graph View — Interactive force-directed graph showing spec-change relationships
  • Full-text Search — Search across all specs and changes
  • Spec Diff — Compare current spec content against historical change versions
  • Live Reload — Automatically refreshes when openspec files change on disk
  • Collapsible Tree Navigator — A Specs / Changes tree sits above the viewer. Hide it from the tool window title bar or the gear menu to give the viewer the whole tool window; the choice and the split ratio are remembered per project
  • Dark / Light Theme — Syncs with your IDE theme

Supported IDEs: IntelliJ IDEA, WebStorm, PyCharm, PhpStorm, GoLand, RubyMine, CLion, Rider, and other IntelliJ-based IDEs (2023.3+)

Getting Started: Open a project that contains an openspec/ directory. The spek tool window will appear in the right sidebar.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.17.0

Search answers the same query the same way spek's other surfaces do. spek implemented search four times, and the four disagreed about what is indexed, what counts as a match and how many results one change may produce. The rule is now stated once and mirrored here in Kotlin, with a shared fixture corpus holding the two implementations in agreement.

  • A change is found by the name its result card shows, so a query copied off a result finds that result.
  • A result comes from the file that actually contains the query. A name match used to be answered by whichever file came first, handing back a snippet with nothing the reader typed in it.
  • Each result says which artifact answered and marks archived changes, so a row explains itself even when there is nothing to highlight in it.
  • Results are ordered with the most recently archived change first, rather than the oldest.
  • A search request with no query is rejected rather than treated as an empty search, matching the web server.
  • Task text and every root artifact file are indexed from the same listing the tabs come from.
